title: Part 3, Chapter 1
paragraphs: Raskolnikov sat up on the sofa. He waved weakly at Razumihin to stop the stream of warm, incoherent reassurances he was directing at his mother and sister, took them both by the hand, and for a minute or two gazed from one to the other in silence. His mother was alarmed by his expression. It showed an agonizingly intense emotion and at the same time something rigid, almost unhinged. Pulcheria Alexandrovna began to cry.
Avdotya Romanovna was pale. Her hand trembled in her brother's.
"Go home... with him," he said in a broken voice, pointing to Razumihin. "Goodbye until tomorrow. Tomorrow -- everything.... How long have you been here?"
"We arrived this evening, Rodya," Pulcheria Alexandrovna answered. "The train was terribly late. But, Rodya, nothing could make me leave you now! I will spend the night here, beside you..."
"Do not torture me!" he said with an irritable gesture.
"I will stay with him," Razumihin cried. "I will not leave him for a second. To hell with all my guests! Let them rage all they want! My uncle is running the show up there."
"How can I ever thank you!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna began, pressing Razumihin's hands again, but Raskolnikov cut her off.
"I cannot stand it! I cannot stand it!" he repeated irritably. "Stop badgering me! Enough -- go away... I cannot take it!"
"Come, Mama, let us step out of the room at least for a moment," Dounia whispered in dismay. "We are clearly upsetting him."
"Can I not even look at him after three years?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna wept.
"Wait," he stopped them again. "You keep interrupting me and my thoughts get muddled.... Have you seen Luzhin?"
"No, Rodya, but he already knows we have arrived. We heard, Rodya, that Pyotr Petrovitch was kind enough to visit you today," Pulcheria Alexandrovna added timidly.
"Yes... he was so kind.... Dounia, I promised Luzhin I would throw him down the stairs and told him to go to hell...."
"Rodya, what are you saying! Surely you do not mean..." Pulcheria Alexandrovna began in alarm, but she stopped, looking at Dounia.

Avdotya Romanovna was watching her brother attentively, waiting for what would come next. Both of them had heard about the quarrel from Nastasya, who had understood and reported what she could, and they were in painful uncertainty and suspense.
"Dounia," Raskolnikov continued with effort, "I do not want this marriage. So tomorrow, at the first opportunity, you must refuse Luzhin. I never want to hear his name again."
"Good heavens!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
"Brother, think about what you are saying!" Avdotya Romanovna began sharply, but immediately caught herself. "You are not fit to talk now. Perhaps you are tired," she added gently.

"You think I am delirious? No.... You are marrying Luzhin for _my_ sake. But I will not accept the sacrifice. So write a letter before tomorrow refusing him... let me read it in the morning, and that will be the end of it!"
"I cannot do that!" the girl cried, offended. "What right do you have--"
"Dounia, you are being hasty too. Be quiet -- tomorrow... Do you not see..." the mother intervened anxiously. "We had better go!"

"He is raving," Razumihin declared tipsily. "How else would he dare! Tomorrow all this nonsense will blow over... though today he really did throw him out. That much is true. And Luzhin got angry too.... He showed up here, tried to show off his learning, and left with his tail between his legs...."
"So it is true?" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
"Goodbye until tomorrow, brother," Dounia said with compassion. "Let us go, Mama... Goodbye, Rodya."

"Listen, sister," he called after them, making one last effort. "I am not delirious. This marriage is an abomination. Let me be a scoundrel, but you must not... one scoundrel is enough... and even though I am a scoundrel, I would not claim such a sister. It is me or Luzhin! Go now...."

"You are out of your mind! Tyrant!" Razumihin roared. But Raskolnikov did not answer -- perhaps could not. He lay down on the sofa and turned to the wall, completely spent. Avdotya Romanovna looked at Razumihin with interest. Her dark eyes flashed. Razumihin actually flinched under her gaze.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna stood there, overwhelmed.
"Nothing could make me leave," she whispered desperately to Razumihin. "I will stay somewhere here... Please take Dounia home."

"You will ruin everything," Razumihin whispered back, losing patience. "Come out to the stairs at least. Nastasya, bring a light! I promise you," he went on in a half whisper on the stairs, "he nearly beat up the doctor and me this afternoon! You understand? The doctor himself backed down and left, so as not to provoke him. I stayed downstairs standing guard, but he got dressed and slipped out anyway. And he will do it again if you upset him -- at this hour of night -- and do himself harm...."
"What are you saying?"

"And Avdotya Romanovna certainly cannot be left alone in those lodgings without you. Just think about where you are staying! That scoundrel Pyotr Petrovitch could not find you anything better... But you know I have had a few drinks, that is why I am... cursing. Do not mind it...."
"But I will go to the landlady here," Pulcheria Alexandrovna insisted. "I will beg her to find some corner for Dounia and me for the night. I cannot leave him like this -- I cannot!"

This conversation took place on the landing just outside the landlady's door. Nastasya lit the way from a step below. Razumihin was in a state of extraordinary excitement. Half an hour earlier, walking Raskolnikov home, he had indeed been talking too much and too freely -- and he knew it -- but his head was clear despite the vast amount he had consumed. Now he was in a state bordering on ecstasy, and everything he had drunk seemed to hit him with redoubled force. He stood with the two ladies, gripping both their hands, trying to persuade them and making his case with astonishing directness of speech. At nearly every word, probably to emphasize his points, he squeezed their hands painfully, as in a vise. He stared at Avdotya Romanovna without the slightest regard for propriety. They sometimes pulled their hands free from his huge bony paws, but far from noticing anything wrong, he only pulled them closer. If they had told him to throw himself headfirst down the staircase, he would have done it without a second thought. Pulcheria Alexandrovna felt the young man was a bit too eccentric and pinched her hand too hard, but in her anxiety about Rodya she saw his presence as providential and was unwilling to take notice of his peculiarities. Avdotya Romanovna shared her worry and was not timid by nature, but she could hardly look at the blazing light in his eyes without wonder and almost alarm. Only the boundless trust inspired by Nastasya's account of her brother's odd friend kept her from trying to run away from him or drag her mother along. She also realized that running was probably impossible now. Ten minutes later, however, she felt considerably calmer. It was characteristic of Razumihin that he showed his true nature instantly, whatever mood he was in, so people quickly saw the kind of man they were dealing with.

"You cannot go to the landlady -- that would be absurd!" he cried. "Even if you are his mother, staying here will drive him to a frenzy, and then God knows what will happen! Listen, here is what I will do. Nastasya will sit with him now, and I will escort you both home. You cannot be out on the streets alone -- Petersburg is a terrible place for that.... But never mind! Then I will run straight back here, and in fifteen minutes, on my word of honor, I will bring you a report on how he is, whether he is sleeping, and everything. Then -- listen! -- I will dash home -- I have a houseful of guests, all drunk -- grab Zossimov, that is the doctor who is treating him, he is there too, but he is not drunk, he is never drunk -- and drag him to Rodya, and then straight to you. So you will get two reports within the hour -- one from the doctor, you understand, from the doctor himself, which is a very different thing from my account. If anything is wrong, I swear I will bring you here myself. But if everything is fine, you go to bed. And I will spend the night here in the hallway -- he will not hear me -- and I will have Zossimov sleep at the landlady's, to be on hand. So what is better for him right now -- you or the doctor? The doctor is obviously more useful. So go home! But the landlady is out of the question. It is fine for me, but not for you. She would not take you anyway, because she is... because she is a fool... She would be jealous of me on account of Avdotya Romanovna, and of you too, if you want to know... definitely of Avdotya Romanovna. She is an absolutely, utterly unaccountable character! Though I am a fool too!... Never mind! Come on! Do you trust me? Well, do you trust me or not?"
"Let us go, Mama," said Avdotya Romanovna. "He will certainly do what he has promised. He has already saved Rodya, and if the doctor really will agree to spend the night here, what could be better?"
"You see -- you understand me, because you are an angel!" Razumihin cried in ecstasy. "Let us go! Nastasya! Run upstairs and sit with him -- with a light. I will be back in fifteen minutes."

Pulcheria Alexandrovna was not entirely convinced, but she made no further objection. Razumihin gave each of them an arm and led them down the stairs. He still worried her, though -- he was clearly capable and good-hearted, but was he really in any condition to carry out his promises? He seemed in such a state....

"I see what you are thinking -- that I am in such a state!" Razumihin broke in on her thoughts, guessing them, as he strode along the pavement with enormous steps, so that both ladies could barely keep up -- a fact he did not notice. "Nonsense! That is... I am drunk like a fool, but that is not the point. It is not the wine that has gone to my head. It is seeing you.... But do not mind me! Do not pay attention. I am talking rubbish, I am unworthy of you.... I am utterly unworthy of you! The minute I have taken you home, I am going to pour two buckets of water over my head at the gutter, and then I will be fine.... If only you knew how I love you both! Do not laugh, and do not be angry! You can be angry with anyone, but not with me! I am his friend, so I am your friend too. I want to be... I had a feeling... Last year there was a moment... well, it was not really a premonition, because you seem to have fallen from heaven. And I probably will not sleep all night... Zossimov was a little worried earlier that he might go mad... that is why he must not be agitated."
"What did you say?" cried the mother.
"Did the doctor really say that?" asked Avdotya Romanovna, alarmed.

"Yes, but it is not true, not one bit. He gave him some medicine, a powder -- I saw it -- and then your arrival.... It would have been better if you had come tomorrow. It is a good thing we left. And in an hour Zossimov himself will report to you about everything. He is not drunk! And I will not be drunk either.... Why did I get so plastered? Because they dragged me into an argument, damn them! I have sworn off arguing! They talk such garbage! I nearly came to blows! I left my uncle there to preside. Would you believe it -- they insist on the complete elimination of individuality, and that is precisely what delights them! Not to be themselves, to be as unlike themselves as possible. That is what they consider the pinnacle of progress. If only their nonsense were their own -- but it is not..."
"Listen!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna interrupted timidly, but this only added fuel to the flames.

"What do you think?" Razumihin shouted, louder than ever. "You think I am attacking them for talking nonsense? Not at all! I like them to talk nonsense. That is humanity's one privilege over all creation. Through error you come to the truth! I am a man because I err! You never reach any truth without making fourteen mistakes -- and very likely a hundred and fourteen. And that is a fine thing in its way. But we cannot even make mistakes on our own! Talk nonsense, but talk _your own_ nonsense, and I will kiss you for it. To go wrong in your own way is better than to go right in someone else's. In the first case you are a person. In the second you are no better than a bird. Truth will not escape you, but life can be choked. There have been examples. And what are we doing now? In science, development, thought, invention, ideals, ambitions, liberalism, judgment, experience -- in everything, everything, everything -- we are still in the preparatory class. We prefer to live on other people's ideas. It is what we are used to! Am I right? Am I right?" cried Razumihin, squeezing and shaking both ladies' hands.
"Oh, mercy -- I really do not know," poor Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried.
"Yes, yes... though I do not agree with everything you say," Avdotya Romanovna added sincerely, and then let out a cry as he squeezed her hand so painfully.

"Yes? You say yes? Well, after that you... you..." he cried in rapture, "you are a fountain of goodness, purity, reason... and perfection! Give me your hand... and yours too! I want to kiss your hands, right here, on my knees..." and he dropped to his knees on the pavement, which was fortunately deserted at that hour.
"Stop -- please, what are you doing?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna exclaimed, thoroughly distressed.
"Get up, get up!" Dounia said, laughing despite her own alarm.

"Not until you let me kiss your hands! There! Enough! I am getting up, and we go on! I am a wretched fool, I am unworthy of you, and drunk besides... and I am ashamed.... I am not worthy of loving you, but to pay you homage is the duty of every man who is not an utter beast! And I have paid homage.... Here are your lodgings, and for that alone Rodya was right to throw your Pyotr Petrovitch out! How dare he! How dare he put you in a place like this? It is outrageous! Do you know what kind of people they take in here? And you -- his fiancee! You are his fiancee, yes? Well then, I will tell you -- your _fiance_ is a scoundrel."
"Mr. Razumihin, you are forgetting yourself..." Pulcheria Alexandrovna began.

"Yes, yes, you are right, I did forget myself. I am ashamed of it," Razumihin hastened to apologize. "But... but you cannot be angry with me for speaking this way! Because I am being sincere, and not because... hmm, hmm! That would be disgraceful. In short, not because I... hmm! Let us leave it at that. I do not dare say why. I dare not.... But we all saw today when he walked in that this man is not one of us. Not because he had his hair curled at the barber's, not because he was in such a hurry to show off his intellect -- but because he is a spy, a speculator, a skinflint, and a buffoon. That is obvious. Do you think he is clever? No -- he is a fool. And is he a match for you? Good God! You see, ladies," he stopped suddenly on the way up to their rooms, "my friends back there are all drunk, every one of them, but they are all honest, and even though we do talk rubbish -- including me -- we will eventually talk our way to the truth, because we are on the right path. Pyotr Petrovitch... is not on the right path. Even though I just called them every name in the book, I do respect them all... and though I do not respect Zametov, I like him because he is just a puppy. And I even like that ox Zossimov, because he is honest and knows his craft. But enough -- all said and forgiven. Is it forgiven? Good, let us go on. I know this corridor. I have been here before -- there was a scandal in number three.... Where are you? Which number? Eight? Well, lock yourselves in for the night. Do not let anyone in. I will be back with news in fifteen minutes, and half an hour after that with Zossimov. You will see! Goodbye! I am off!"
"Good heavens, Dounia, what is going to happen?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna said to her daughter, anxious and dismayed.

"Do not worry, Mama," said Dounia, taking off her hat and cape. "God sent this man to help us, even if he has come from a drinking party. We can count on him, I am sure. And everything he has done for Rodya..."

"Oh, Dounia -- who knows if he will even come back! How could I bring myself to leave Rodya?... And how different, how different this was from the meeting I had imagined! He was so sullen, as though he was not even glad to see us...."
Tears came to her eyes.
"No, that is not it, Mama. You did not see clearly -- you were crying the whole time. He is completely unhinged by a serious illness. That is all it is."

"Oh, this illness! What is going to happen? And the way he spoke to you, Dounia!" the mother said, looking timidly at her daughter and trying to read her thoughts, already half-consoled by Dounia's willingness to defend her brother, which meant she had already forgiven him. "I am sure he will think better of it tomorrow," she added, probing further.

"And I am sure he will say exactly the same thing tomorrow... about _that_," Avdotya Romanovna said firmly. And there was nothing more to say, because this was the point Pulcheria Alexandrovna was afraid to discuss. Dounia went to her mother and kissed her. The mother embraced her tightly without a word. Then she sat down to wait anxiously for Razumihin's return, timidly watching her daughter pace the room with folded arms, lost in thought. This pacing while thinking was a habit of Avdotya Romanovna's, and her mother was always afraid to interrupt her at such moments.

Razumihin's sudden, drunken infatuation with Avdotya Romanovna was, of course, ridiculous. But anyone seeing her just then -- walking back and forth, arms folded, pensive and melancholy -- might well have understood it, eccentric state or not. Avdotya Romanovna was remarkably good-looking: tall, strikingly proportioned, strong, and self-assured -- a quality apparent in every gesture, though it in no way detracted from the grace and softness of her movements. In face she resembled her brother, but she could genuinely be called beautiful. Her hair was dark brown, a shade lighter than her brother's. There was a proud light in her nearly black eyes, and yet at times they showed extraordinary kindness. She was pale, but it was a healthy pallor. Her face radiated freshness and vitality. Her mouth was rather small; the full red lower lip protruded slightly, as did her chin -- the only irregularity in her beautiful face, but it gave her a distinctly individual, almost haughty expression. Her face was always more serious and thoughtful than cheerful. But how well laughter suited it -- youthful, lighthearted, carefree laughter! It was natural enough that a warm, open, honest giant like Razumihin, who had never seen anyone like her and was not entirely sober, should lose his head immediately. Besides, as fate would have it, he first saw Dounia transfigured by her love for her brother and her joy at meeting him. Then he watched her lower lip quiver with indignation at her brother's arrogant, cruel, ungrateful words -- and his fate was sealed.

He had spoken the truth, moreover, when he let slip in his drunken rambling on the stairs that the eccentric landlady Praskovya Pavlovna would be jealous of Pulcheria Alexandrovna as well as Avdotya Romanovna on his account. Although Pulcheria Alexandrovna was forty-three, her face still bore traces of its former beauty. She looked much younger than her years, as is almost always the case with women who retain serenity of spirit, warmth of heart, and pure, sincere feeling into old age. We might add in passing that preserving these qualities is the only way to preserve beauty as well. Her hair had begun to turn grey and thin, little crow's-feet had long since appeared around her eyes, and her cheeks were hollow and sunken from worry and grief -- yet it was still a handsome face. She was Dounia over again, twenty years later, minus the protruding lower lip. Pulcheria Alexandrovna was emotional but not sentimental, timid and yielding -- but only up to a point. She could give way and accept a great deal, even things contrary to her convictions, but there was a line defined by honesty, principle, and her deepest beliefs that nothing in the world could make her cross.
Exactly twenty minutes after Razumihin left, there came two soft but hurried knocks at the door: he was back.

"I will not come in -- I do not have time," he said quickly when the door opened. "He is sleeping like a log -- soundly, peacefully. God willing, he will sleep ten hours. Nastasya is with him. I told her not to leave until I return. Now I am off to fetch Zossimov. He will give you his report and then you should turn in. I can see you are too exhausted to do anything..."
And he ran off down the corridor.
"What a very capable and... devoted young man!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna exclaimed, thoroughly delighted.
"He seems like a wonderful person!" Avdotya Romanovna replied with some warmth, resuming her walk around the room.

Nearly an hour later they heard footsteps in the corridor and another knock. Both women waited, this time with complete confidence in Razumihin's promise. He had indeed managed to bring Zossimov. Zossimov had agreed without hesitation to leave the party and see Raskolnikov, but he came to the ladies' door reluctantly and with deep suspicion, not trusting Razumihin's judgment in his exhilarated condition. But his vanity was instantly reassured and flattered: he saw they really were expecting him like an oracle. He stayed exactly ten minutes and succeeded in completely reassuring and comforting Pulcheria Alexandrovna. He spoke with evident sympathy but with the reserve and exaggerated seriousness of a young doctor at an important consultation. He did not utter a word on any other subject and showed no desire whatever to enter into more personal relations with the two ladies. Noting Avdotya Romanovna's dazzling beauty the moment he walked in, he made every effort to ignore her throughout, addressing himself solely to Pulcheria Alexandrovna. All of this gave him enormous inner satisfaction. He declared that in his opinion the patient was currently progressing very satisfactorily. His observations indicated that the illness was due partly to the patient's unfortunate material circumstances over recent months, but also had a moral dimension -- was, so to speak, the product of multiple material and psychological influences, anxieties, fears, worries, certain obsessive ideas, and so forth. Noticing out of the corner of his eye that Avdotya Romanovna was following every word closely, Zossimov allowed himself to expand on this theme. When Pulcheria Alexandrovna anxiously and timidly asked whether there was "any suspicion of insanity," he answered with a calm, candid smile that his words had been exaggerated. The patient certainly showed signs of a fixed idea, something approaching monomania -- he, Zossimov, was particularly studying this fascinating branch of medicine -- but it should be remembered that until today the patient had been delirious, and the arrival of his family would undoubtedly have a beneficial effect on his recovery and provide distraction, "provided all new upsets can be avoided," he added significantly. Then he rose, took his leave with an impressive and gracious bow, and departed amid blessings, warm gratitude, and entreaties. Avdotya Romanovna spontaneously offered him her hand. He left exceedingly pleased with his visit and even more so with himself.
"We will talk tomorrow. Go to bed now!" Razumihin said in parting, following Zossimov out. "I will be back first thing in the morning with my report."
"What a charming girl that Avdotya Romanovna is," Zossimov remarked, practically licking his lips as they stepped into the street.

"Charming? You said charming?" Razumihin roared, and he flew at Zossimov and seized him by the throat. "If you ever dare.... Do you understand? Do you understand?" he shouted, shaking him by the collar and pinning him to the wall. "Do you hear me?"

"Let go, you drunken maniac," Zossimov said, struggling free. When Razumihin released him, Zossimov stared at him for a moment and then burst out laughing. Razumihin stood facing him, brooding and grimly serious.
"Of course I am an ass," he said, dark as a thundercloud. "But still... so are you."
"No, brother, not at all. I am not dreaming of anything foolish."
They walked on in silence, and only when they were nearly at Raskolnikov's building did Razumihin break it, clearly troubled.

"Listen," he said. "You are a good fellow, but among your other faults you are a ladies' man -- I know it -- and a filthy one at that. You are a weak, nervous wreck and a bundle of whims. You are getting fat and lazy and cannot deny yourself anything -- and I call that filthy because it leads straight into the gutter. You have let yourself go so badly that I honestly do not know how you are still a good -- even a dedicated -- doctor. You sleep on a featherbed and get up at night for your patients! In another three or four years you will not bother getting up at all... But to hell with all that, that is not the point.... You are going to spend tonight in the landlady's apartment here. (It took some doing to persuade her!) And I will be in the kitchen. So here is your chance to get to know her better.... It is not what you think! Not a trace of anything like that, brother...!"
"But I do not think anything!"

"Here you have modesty, brother -- silence, bashfulness, fierce virtue... and yet she is melting, simply melting like wax! Save me from her, for the love of God! She is extremely attractive... I will repay you, I will do anything...."
Zossimov laughed harder than ever.
"Well, you are smitten! But what am I supposed to do with her?"

"It will not be any trouble, I promise. Just talk to her -- say whatever you like, as long as you sit next to her and talk. You are a doctor besides -- try treating her for something. I swear you will not regret it. She has a piano, and you know I play a little. I have a song there, a real Russian one: 'I shed hot tears.' She loves the genuine article -- and well, it all started with that song. You are a real performer though, a master, a Rubinstein.... I guarantee you will not regret it!"
"Have you made her some promise? Signed something? A promise of marriage?"
"Nothing, nothing, absolutely nothing of the sort! Besides, she is not that type at all.... Tchebarov tried that approach...."
"Then just drop her!"
"But I cannot just drop her!"
"Why not?"
"Well, I just cannot, that is all! There is an element of... attraction here, brother."
"Then why did you lead her on?"

"I did not lead her on! Maybe I was the one who was led on, in my foolishness. But she will not care whether it is you or me -- as long as somebody sits beside her and sighs.... I cannot explain the situation, brother... Look, you are good at mathematics, and you are working on it now -- start teaching her integral calculus! I am serious, completely serious. It will be all the same to her. She will gaze at you and sigh for a whole year. I talked to her once for two days straight about the Prussian House of Lords -- you have to talk about _something_ -- and she just sighed and sweated! And you must not talk about love -- she is bashful to the point of hysteria -- but make it clear you cannot tear yourself away. That is all it takes. It is incredibly comfortable -- you are completely at home. You can read, sit, lounge around, write. You might even risk a kiss, if you are careful."
"But what do I want with her?"

"Oh, I cannot make you see! Look -- you two are made for each other! I have thought of you many times!... You will end up there eventually! So what difference does it make whether it is sooner or later? There is the featherbed factor, brother -- oh, and not only that! There is a pull here -- here you have the end of the world, a safe harbor, a quiet anchorage, the center of the earth, the three fish that support the world, the essence of pancakes, of rich fish pies, of the evening samovar, of soft sighs and warm shawls, of heated stoves to sleep on -- as cozy as being dead, except you are alive -- the best of both worlds! Well, to hell with it, brother, I am talking rubbish. Time for bed! Listen -- I sometimes wake in the night, so I will go check on him. But there is no need really -- everything is fine. Do not worry yourself. But if you feel like it, you could look in on him once too. If you notice anything -- delirium, fever -- wake me at once. But there should not be anything."
